newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Bumper grains crop seen despite weather.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bumper grains crop seen despite weather.

text.p: Rain, or the lack of it, has forced analysts to cut estimates for cereals production in many parts of the world but good performances in a handful of countries, particularly the U.S., mean that 1997 will see another bumper harvest.
The world will produce a total of 1,480 million tonnes of grain this year compared with 1,479 million tonnes in 1996, according to the London-based International Grains Council.

The IGC, an authoritative monitor of the world cereals market, revised its estimate for U.S. wheat production up as it became clear that cold weather in April was offset by near perfect conditions since.
A month ago the IGC saw U.S. wheat production at 60 million tonnes. Now it is looking for 62.6 million, an increase on last year's 62.1 million tonnes.

Warmer weather since the end of June also benefitted the U.S. maize crop, the IGC said in a report issued on Thursday. Its crop estimate for U.S. maize is 250 million tonnes, 14 million more than last year. Industry sources noted a large increase in the number of animals fed on maize in the U.S.

But weather has caused problems elsewhere. Estimates of Australian wheat production have been cut following reports of poor growing conditions. The IGC now puts the Australian wheat crop at 16.5 million tonnes compared with an earlier estimate of 18 million. Last year's crop was 23.5 million tonnes.
For Australia, the problem is El Nino, a warm water current in the Pacific Ocean which has a widespread effect on southern hemisphere weather.
A shortage of rain caused a cut in expected wheat production in Morocco, while too much rain had delayed planting in Argentina.

Recent rains in Europe promoted wheat growth in northern parts of the EU, reeling from a record dry start to the year. But the same rain is now delaying the French barley harvest. And it is still too hot and dry for crops in Spain, Italy and Portugal.
Not enough rain has slowed maize planting in parts of China.
One of the IGC's biggest production cuts was for Canada's wheat crop, now seen at 25.5 million tonnes from 27 million forecast a month ago, but this was not because of the weather.
Canadian farmers reduced wheat plantings for simple economic reasons. Other crops, including canola and flaxseed, are more profitable, the IGC said.
The IGC cut its prediction for 1997-98 Canadian wheat exports to 19.5 million tonnes from an earlier estimate of 20.0 million. But this is still well up on the previous year's 17.2 million tonnes.

It left its estimates for other major exporters unchanged, which means Argentina would export 8.5 million tonnes compared with 10.5 in 1996-97, Australia 15.5 million (17.8), EU 16 million (16) and the U.S. 27.5 million (26.5 million).

A good maize crop will help the U.S. maintain its dominant position in exports of coarse grains (maize, barley, sorghum, oats and rye). It is expected to export 57 million tonnes in 1997-98 out of a total 91.7 million. In 1996-97 the U.S. accounted for 52.6 million tonnes of world exports of 88.8 million, according to the IGC.
